newsitem.title: UK: Ex-UK air cargo eyes surcharges/capacity lift to April 1.
newsitem.headline: Ex-UK air cargo eyes surcharges/capacity lift to April 1.

text.p: Surcharges moved back to the top of the agenda in the ex-UK air cargo market on Thursday after Virgin Atlantic said it was dropping its fuel surcharge from April one, a Reuters survey showed.

Export business from the UK has been good and has held air cargo rates from the UK across the Atlantic steady but there are fears they could fall once capacity increases with when summer schedules come into operation on April 1.

News on Thursday morning that Virgin was following the move two weeks ago by Delta Air Lines to drop cargo surcharges fuelled speculation that some of the major freight carriers would soon make similar moves. Delta was the first to drop the surcharges imposed last November after jet fuel prices surged.
Most surcharges were set at 10 cents per kilo or the local currency equivalent on long haul and 5 cents on European or short haul flights.

Many in the cargo industry now expect surcharges may drop soon especially as prices are now the lowest since last July. But others said last summer's fuel prices were still historically high and they still hoped to maintain a surcharge until prices dipped further.

Overseas carriers flying from the UK, forwarders and shippers are all closely watching BA to see if it shifts its position on surcharges. Earlier this week a BA spokesman said surcharges remain continually under review.
Some sources said it will take a major European freight carrier like BA or Lufthansa LHAG.FA, Air France or KLM to drop its fuel surcharge before others fall in line.
"Delta by itself is not big enough to bring its (the surcharge) removal," said a source at one carrier.
"I hope it does not go as it provides extra revenue for us although I wouldn't like to try to justify it," said one firm specialising in buying spare cargo capacity.
Business from the UK has remained busy up to the long four day Easter holiday weekend and this has kept rates stable.
"U.S. importers seem to be filling their warehouses," said one forwarder but he expected a slowdown next week.

Looking to the increased bellyhold capacity available soon available to Miami, one forwarder said current rates are "not sustainable". Rates are now as low as 60 pence a kilo for 100 kilo loads with one tonne bookings as much as 10 pence lower depending on carrier.

This weekend's Brazilian Grand Prix has meant extra cargo for scheduled carriers flying to Rio although the actual racing cars going to the various international circuits usually travel in specially chartered 747 organised by the Italian based motor sports division of MSAS. For example Varig's UK cargo manager Paul Ryan said it had taken a ten tonne load of spares to Rio for Sunday's race.

Although many headline rates cargo go up from Monday April 1 this is accompanied by increased capacity rates so that several carriers on the transatlantic and Latin American routes said they would not be surprised to see rates lower by mid-April.

The battle for cargo on the competitive North Atlantic route has been underlined by the further extension of BA's special promotion of pallet rates. These have been running all year and have given forwarders and shippers taking whole pallets a discount of some 30 percent over weight rates.

Earlier this week BA said the special promotion would be continued into April but details were not available on Thursday. The promotion in second half March covered against 55 routes in the second halve of March.

Some carriers and forwarders said they doubted if there will be enough cargo in the next few months to absorb the extra capacity in the summer schedules that begin to come into effect next week. But a number of carriers are more optimistic.

Some carriers are also mixed in their attitude to raising rates now as they believe underlying business is not strong enough to justify pushing rates upwards. Iberian's 's UK cargo sales manager Enrique Sagra said the suspension of Venezuela's Viasa airline has placed pressure on capacity and it has had to fit in what it can in flights via Madrid. Since 1991 Iberia has owned 45 percent of Viasa.
The recent move by Air Canada OCT. to impose penalties on weekend "no shows" has nearly eliminated the failure of forwarders to forewarn carriers of cargoes that cannot take booked space.
An Air Canada official said that cancellations on last Friday had been reallocated leaving just one 100 kilo order that did not show resulting in a 50 percent penalty charge.
"No shows have virtually disappeared," an Air Canada official said.
"March has been a good month and we've been very busy at weekends especially with perishables transhipped through London from Israel and Amsterdam," the Air Canada official stated.

Other recent Air Canada business has included aircraft parts from Belfast's Short Brothers being flown from Heathrow to Bombardier in Canada ,Rolls Royce engines flown to Vancouver for trucking to Boeing in Seattle and Irish computer parts destined for Canada.
Extra Air Canada capacity includes a new daily A340 London-Calgary flight which is being introduced to meet passenger demand.
Air Canada's UK and Ireland cargo manager Mike Judkins said flights to Calgary and Halifax have space but those to Montreal and Toronto are full.

Specialist cargo carrier Heavylift has recently carried two satellites from France and one from the U.S. to French Guiana on its Antonov 124's, said its managing director Michael Hayles. - Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+5017
